extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques and elementary discrete mathematics (induction, number theory, relations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked examples for common undergraduate proof techniques (proof by smallest counterexample, (strong) induction) and elementary theory of relations (definitions, reflexive/symmetric/transitive properties, equivalence relations and classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by Smallest Counterexample (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition: The statements S1, S2, S3, S4, . . . are all true. Proof (Smallest counterexample): (1) Check that the first statement S1 is true. (2) For the sake of contradiction, suppose not every Sn is true. (3) Let k > 1 be the smallest integer for which Sk is false. (4) Then Sk−1 is true and Sk is false. Use this to get a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use steps (1)–(4) as a template: verify the base case, assume a counterexample exists, pick the minimal counterexample k, exploit the fact Sk−1 (or some earlier statement) is true while Sk is false to derive a contradiction. The text demonstrates this with the example proving 4 | (5^n − 1). Note: writers often omit explicit statement of the technique; you may need to glean it from the structure where a smallest counterexample is chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Induction to Prove Existence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a property for every integer ≥ 2: use strong induction with a basis step (e.g., n=2) and the inductive hypothesis that every integer between 2 and n (inclusive) has the property; then prove it for n+1 by expressing n+1 in terms of smaller integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: existence of a prime factorization for every integer > 1: basis n=2, assume every integer ≤ n has a prime factorization, consider n+1: if prime done, otherwise factor n+1 = ab with a,b < n+1 and use factorizations of a and b. Use strong induction when the step for n+1 depends on multiple earlier cases, not just n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Smallest Counterexample to Prove Uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness of a decomposition (e.g., prime factorization), assume for contradiction there exists a smallest n with two distinct factorizations, then show a prime factor in one factorization must equal a prime factor in the other, cancel it to get a smaller counterexample, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: uniqueness of prime factorization: choose smallest n with two distinct prime factorizations, show p1 divides product of ai so equals some ai (since ai prime), cancel and obtain a smaller number with two distinct factorizations, contradicting minimality. This combines minimal-counterexample reasoning with divisibility facts (Proposition that a prime dividing a product divides one factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: General structure of an induction proof (base + inductive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction proof should verify a base case (e.g., n=1 or n=2) and then prove that assuming the statement for k (or for all ≤ k in strong induction) implies the statement for k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing an inductive proof number the logical steps (basis, inductive hypothesis, inductive step) even if numbering is not required; manipulate algebraic relations to reduce the k+1 case to earlier cases. The Fibonacci examples illustrate algebraic manipulations using recurrence Fn = Fn−1 + Fn−2 in the inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proving properties about sequences use the recurrence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences defined by a recurrence (e.g., Fibonacci Fn = Fn−1 + Fn−2), expect to use that defining recurrence somewhere in the inductive proof to relate Fn+1 to earlier terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Fibonacci proofs the identity Fn = Fn−1 + Fn−2 is the natural tool for inductive steps; the text emphasizes that the recurrence is the 'perfect setup for induction'. Examples: proving algebraic identities involving Fn via expansion and substitution of recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert: proof technique may be unstated
rubrics_metrics.description: In other textbooks or papers, writers often do not tell you up front which proof technique is being used; you must read through proofs to glean from context which technique is being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop ability to analyze proofs and recognize patterns (e.g., minimal counterexample, induction, contradiction) from structure rather than explicit labels. The text warns this is normal and part of learning mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing a relation as a subset of A×A (definition of relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation on a set A is a subset R ⊆ A × A. The statement (x, y) ∈ R is abbreviated x R y; (x, y) ∉ R is abbreviated x (not R) y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can represent relations by listing ordered pairs, by set-builder notation, or by diagrams (arrows between nodes). Any subset of A×A qualifies as a relation, even if it has no intuitive semantic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to describe/visualize relations (ordered pairs, diagrams, set-builder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations can be encoded as lists of ordered pairs, as set-builder expressions (e.g., {(x,y) in Z×Z : x−y ∈ nZ}), or drawn as directed graphs with nodes and arrows representing (x,y) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams for small finite sets to spot properties quickly; use set-builder notation for infinite relations. Pictures have limitations — cannot draw infinite relations — but are useful for intuition and spotting loops/two-way arrows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and checking of reflexive property
rubrics_metrics.description: R is reflexive if x R x for every x ∈ A (i.e., ∀x ∈ A, xRx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In diagrams reflexivity corresponds to a loop at each node. To prove reflexivity directly, show for arbitrary x that xRx (e.g., for ≡ (mod n) note n | (x−x) so x ≡ x (mod n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and checking of symmetric property
rubrics_metrics.description: R is symmetric if xR y implies yR x for all x, y ∈ A (i.e., ∀x,y ∈ A, xRy ⇒ yRx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In diagrams symmetry corresponds to every arrow having a matching arrow in the opposite direction. To prove symmetry use direct argument (e.g., for congruence modulo n: n | (x−y) ⇒ n | (y−x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and checking of transitive property
rubrics_metrics.description: R is transitive if whenever xR y and yR z, then also xR z (i.e., ∀x,y,z ∈ A, (xRy ∧ yRz) ⇒ xRz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In diagrams transitivity corresponds to whenever there is an arrow x→y and y→z there must be an arrow x→z. Prove by combining the hypotheses (e.g., for ≡ (mod n) add divisibility relations). Note: when x=y=z special-case yields loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotting properties from diagrams (visual tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflexivity ↔ loop at every point; Symmetry ↔ every arrow x→y accompanied by y→x; Transitivity ↔ whenever arrows x→y and y→z exist there is an arrow x→z (and consequently loops at x and y in some symmetric cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides pictorial templates showing what to look for. Use these visual checks for small finite relations to quickly decide whether properties hold; for infinite relations rely on algebraic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation: characterization and checking
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check a relation is an equivalence relation verify the three properties. Examples: equality, congruence modulo n, parity-based relations. Equivalence relations partition the set into disjoint equivalence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class definition and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A and an element a ∈ A, the equivalence class [a] = { x ∈ A : x R a } is the subset of elements related to a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence classes form a partition of A: if [a] and [b] intersect nontrivially then they are equal. Examples show how to compute classes (e.g., parity yields two classes). Use classes to reason about 'sameness' under R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving properties of specific relations by direct algebraic arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a concrete relation (e.g., ≡ (mod n) or divisibility) has properties like reflexive/symmetric/transitive, use direct proofs relying on definitions (e.g., divisibility, algebraic manipulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: proof that congruence mod n is reflexive (n|(x−x)), symmetric (n|(x−y) ⇒ n|(y−x)), and transitive (add x−y and y−z to get x−z divisible by n). Use explicit integer equations and closure under addition/multiplication where appropriate.
